newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown reiterates government line on EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown reiterates government line on EMU.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, reiterating the Labour government's position on a single European currency, said Britain would only join if this was in its economic interests.

"The government's concern about the single currency has always been that Britain should only join if the economic decisions are right, not on the basis of a timetable that has been set politically," he said in a speech prepared for delivery to the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
Brown said a single currency could bring the benefit of increased trade and competition, lower transaction costs and lower long-term interest rates.

But Britain would only join if five key tests were met -- would EMU create better conditions for long-term investment in Britain, would it hurt or help Britain's financial services, would the business cycles and economic structures of member countries be compatible, would there be sufficient flexibility in the system to cope with external problems and would it promote higher growth, stability and a lasting increase in jobs?
"In short, the tests represent Britain's national economic interest," Brown said.
He said he wanted to put British proposals for economic reform at the centre of the European agenda.

The proposals were aimed at new policies for opening up competition and completing the single market, a new agenda for employment and employability, new policies on competitiveness and more flexible markets and reform in EU finances.
"We reject both the federal way forward and the regulatory way ahead and in promoting this third way I believe we improve all our prospects for growth, jobs and prosperity in the long term."
